clue.text: Perspective from train, even if stopping regularly

parts.note: to school someone is to train them

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: oft is an old word for often, i.e. regularly
though means even if

explanation.surface: Someone's view on rail travel, stoically holding even when the train halts at every station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' looks like a railway noun but is a verb, to school. 'stopping' means plugging: the 'even if' word fills the 'regularly' word. 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular body of opinion or outlook, as in a line of argument shared by a group of thinkers.

clue.text: Supply inn with hogsheads, now disclosing plans

indicators.note: supply here is the adverb of supple, i.e. flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order

explanation.surface: A publican stocking the inn with barrels of beer, while revealing their business intentions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is read as 'in a supple way', the anagram signal, not as 'provide'. 'with' is a link joining the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from card play: revealing your cards means letting others see your intentions.

clue.text: Judge and posh tax criminal sat next to one another

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent or wrong, so the letters are twisted

parts.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose, so sat gives posed

explanation.surface: A judge and a wealthy tax fraudster were seated side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges TAX into XTA. U as 'posh' comes from the old U and non-U classification of upper-class English usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Juxtaposed things are placed side by side or close together, the adjacency the phrase describes.

clue.text: Potent smell's caught that's representative of pupils

indicators.note: caught means trapped or held, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: a heady drink is a potent one
BO is body odour, an unpleasant smell

explanation.surface: A strong whiff has been detected, and something is said to stand for the students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' means holding the smell inside the potent word. A head boy is the senior boy chosen to lead and speak for pupils in a British school.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools the senior male pupil appointed to lead and speak for the student body.

clue.text: In the current circumstances, fool takes one in

indicators.note: takes, completed by the final in, means absorbs, so one piece goes inside the other
in completes takes ... in, marking the inner piece

parts.note: an ass is a fool
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Given how things stand now, an idiot welcomes someone inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes ... in' puts I inside ASS.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes accepting something exactly in its present state, without alteration or guarantee.

clue.text: English run grim economy badly: things'll get ugly!

indicators.note: badly means poorly done, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A warning that a mismanaged English economy will lead to trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges E with RUNGRIMECONOMY.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchphrase threatening that politeness is over and harsh treatment is coming.

clue.text: 2, perhaps, means 6

definitions.meaning: showing one's hand(s) literally happens when gloves come off, so 2 Down is an example of it
the cross-reference to 6 Down, a phrase announcing that fighting will be ruthless from now on

explanation.surface: A cross-reference teaser linking two other answers in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 2 Down literally: a bare hand is on show once the gloves are removed. Figuratively, the phrase means the same as 6 Down: no more restraint.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxers fought bare-knuckle once gloves came off, so the idiom means a fight with no holds barred.

clue.text: Reserve hotel with flower in cool place

parts.note: ice can mean coldness or reserve of manner
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a flower is something that flows, here the River Ouse in England

explanation.surface: Booking a hotel and bringing blooms to a chilly spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is a river, not a bloom: the Ouse is an English river.
explanation.definitionFit: An old building where ice was stored to keep things chilled before refrigeration existed.

clue.text: Ambassador, found with smut, is calm

indicators.note: found with means accompanying, placing the soot piece first and the ambassador after it

parts.note: smut is a particle of soot or dirt
HE stands for His Excellency, the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: A diplomat caught with dirt on them stays unruffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To soothe is to quieten or pacify, a verb sense of calm.

clue.text: Wader's good sense on westward track

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the sense piece follows the reversed track
in an across clue westward means read right to left

parts.note: to dog is to follow or track
wit is shrewdness or good sense

explanation.surface: A wading bird showing good judgement by heading west on a path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'westward' turns DOG into GOD. 'Wader's' is 'Wader is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-billed shorebird of the sandpiper family that wades in mudflats.

clue.text: Slate masons remove

parts.note: to slate is to criticise harshly, to diss
a lodge is a branch of Freemasons

explanation.surface: Builders working on a slate roof take tiles off.
explanation.definitionFit: To force something out of its position is to shift or eject it.

clue.text: Dash in road, back to the start

indicators.note: the last letter of the word for road goes back to its front

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road

explanation.surface: A sprint along a street before turning back to where you began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to the start' moves the final E of LANE to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash and élan both mean stylish vigour or flair.

clue.text: Landlord's stewed tripe scoffed by approving soldiers

indicators.note: scoffed means eaten, so the stewed dish goes inside the eaters

parts.note: pro means in favour of
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

indicators.note: stewed means cooked and mixed up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An innkeeper's stewed offal is wolfed down by appreciative troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stewed' rearranges the tripe; 'scoffed by' sets it between the approving and soldier pieces. 'Landlord's' is 'Landlord is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An owner of a property or business, such as a pub, is its landlord.

clue.text: Scientist's lady's cross, oppressed by dull routine

indicators.note: in a down clue, oppressed by means sitting beneath, so the routine piece goes on top

parts.note: a rut is a dull routine
her is the possessive for a woman
a ford is a place to cross a river; to ford is to cross

explanation.surface: A woman is angry, weighed down by a tedious daily grind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' is a verb, ford, not anger. Ernest Rutherford was the New Zealand-born physicist who split the atom.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering nuclear physicist, an example of a scientist.

clue.text: Vain fellow with sense to wear jacket of organdie

indicators.note: wearing a jacket means being inside it, so the pieces go within
a jacket is the outside, so the outer letters of organdie are taken

parts.note: nous is common sense

explanation.surface: A conceited man with good taste dons a jacket of fine muslin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jacket of' takes O and E from organdie; F and NOUS go inside. 'Vain' means futile, not conceited.
explanation.definitionFit: A vain attempt is futile, one that achieves nothing.

clue.text: Sulphur and more acid in dish

parts.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
tarter means more sour or acidic

explanation.surface: A chemistry-lab warning about sulphur and stronger acid in a container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dish' looks like a lab vessel; it is food.
explanation.definitionFit: The first course of a meal is a small dish served before the main.

clue.text: Like some leaves having two buds?

definitions.meaning: describing leaves shaped like an open hand, with lobes spreading from one point
two buddies, a pal and a mate, read as one word

explanation.walkthrough: 'buds' looks botanical but means buddies.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanical term for leaves divided into lobes radiating from a centre, like fingers from a palm.

clue.text: Worn after study, lawyers must don article

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the article goes around the other pieces

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: after means the lawyers piece comes following the study piece

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it
the bar is the body of barristers

explanation.surface: After training, barristers are told to put on a particular garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must don' wraps THE round READBAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing worn down so the nap shows through is shabby and thin.

clue.text: Russian front east of Iceland's capital

indicators.note: in an across clue east of means placed to the right, so front follows
a capital letter here is the first letter of the word

parts.note: the van is the front, as in vanguard

explanation.surface: A Russian battle line located east of Reykjavik.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' picks I, not Reykjavik.
explanation.definitionFit: A typical Russian man's name, used as a byword for a Russian.

clue.text: Problem around heroin, with opportunity to shoot up

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the problem word is read backwards

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
H is slang for heroin
room is scope or opportunity, as in room for improvement

explanation.surface: A drug problem involving heroin and an addict with a chance to inject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shoot up' suggests injecting the heroin, but it means to grow rapidly. 'around' reverses the problem word.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow or spread suddenly and rapidly, as fungi spring up overnight.

clue.text: Outstanding poet's encouragement to unite

parts.note: O is the poetic exclamation of address or appeal
to wed is to join or unite

explanation.surface: A distinguished verse-writer urges a couple to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' means unpaid, not excellent. Together the pieces read 'O, wed!', a poet's plea to unite.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt still owing is outstanding, i.e. not yet paid.

clue.text: Bent lawman gets round the law

indicators.note: gets round means encircles, so the lawman's letters surround the law

parts.note: a Fed is a US federal agent
lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: A corrupt officer evades legal rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like corrupt but means curved.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb that has been bent at the joint has been crooked or tensed.

clue.text: Wife gets joint that's beef

parts.note: a hinge is a movable joint

explanation.surface: A wife buys a cut of beef from the butcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beef' and 'joint' suggest meat; beef is slang for a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a grumble or complaint.

clue.text: Pretender wants pastry, having uncovered buffet

parts.note: a tart is a pastry

indicators.note: uncovered means with the outer covering removed, so the first and last letters go

explanation.surface: Someone after a pastry who has found the buffet laid bare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncovered' strips buffet to UFFE. Tartuffe is the religious hypocrite in Molière's comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière's title character is a hypocrite feigning piety, so a byword for an impostor.
